scenes.narration: Loops that build lists are so common that Python has a shortcut. Today we meet the list comprehension.

Fruit goes in, a rule is applied, and a glass comes out for each fruit. Add an if at the end to keep only some items. Keep comprehensions short. If a line is hard to read, write the loop out in full instead.

scenes.onScreen: squares.py: squares of every number, and only the even ones
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A list of five numbers. [HL 2] Read it left to right. For each n in nums, make n times n. The result is a new list of squares. [HL 3] One, four, nine, sixteen, twenty five. [HL 4] Add an if at the end to filter. Keep n only when it divides by two. [HL 5] Two and four.

code.source:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
print(squares)
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

scenes.onScreen: nums, squares and evens each tied to their own list
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. Nums, squares and evens each point at their own list object. A comprehension never changes the source list. It builds a brand new one. Nums is exactly as it was. That is what makes comprehensions safe. You never change the list while you walk over it.

scenes.onScreen: words_comp.py: make capitals and lengths from a list of words
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A list of three words. [HL 2] For each word, call upper. We get a list of capital words. [HL 3] For each word, take its length. A list of numbers. [HL 4] Print the capital words. [HL 5] Print the lengths. Four, four, five. Any expression can go at the front, a method call, a sum, a call to len.

code.source:
words = ["fish", "crab", "prawn"]
caps = [w.upper() for w in words]
lengths = [len(w) for w in words]
print(caps)
print(lengths)

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as words_comp dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, words_comp dot py. Fish, crab, prawn in capitals, then four, four, five.

Four: If a comprehension is hard to read, use a normal loop. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: else in the wrong place
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We try to keep even numbers, and use zero for the rest. We wrote an if with no else before the for. Python says, syntax error, expected else after if expression. A choice between two values needs both if and else, before the for. A simple filter goes at the end, with no else.

props.wrongCode:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
labels = [n if n % 2 == 0 for n in nums]
props.fixedCode:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
labels = [n if n % 2 == 0 else 0 for n in nums]
print(labels)
props.error:
File "squares.py", line 2
    labels = [n if n % 2 == 0 for n in nums]
              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: expected 'else' after 'if' expression

lines: labels = [n if n % 2 == 0 for n in nums]

props.why: An if that picks between two values needs its else, and both sit in front of the for; a filter if without else goes at the end.

shorts.title: One-line loops
shorts.hook: "A list comprehension builds a list in one line."
shorts.script: A list comprehension builds a list in one line. Square brackets, then what you want for each item, then for, the item, in, the source list. Nums squared looks like n times n, for n in nums. It replaces a three line loop with a single line. Read it from left to right, like a sentence, and it makes perfect sense. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A loop in one line.

shorts.title: Filter with if
shorts.hook: "Add an if at the end to keep only some items."
shorts.script: Add an if at the end to keep only some items. Square brackets, n, for n in nums, if n modulo two equals zero. Only the even numbers make it into the new list. The source list is never changed. The if is a filter, and it has no else. It is a neat way to pick the items you want from a long list. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.onScreen: [N FOR N IN NUMS IF N % 2 == 0]
shorts.caption: Keep only what you want.

shorts.title: Keep it readable
shorts.hook: "Comprehensions are great, but do not overuse them."
shorts.script: Comprehensions are great, but do not overuse them. If a comprehension needs two loops, three conditions, and a function call, it is too long. Write a normal loop instead. Then you can read your code later. A good rule is that you should read the line once, and understand it. Short and clear beats clever, every time. Remember that. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Do not be too clever.

shorts.title: If and else placement
shorts.script: Here is the syntax trap. You want even numbers, and zero for the rest. You write an if, with no else, before the for. Python says, syntax error, expected else after if expression. A choice between two values needs both if and else, before the for. A plain filter if goes at the end, and has no else. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Placement matters.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the comprehension get a short job title?"
shorts.script: Why did the comprehension get a short job title? It did everything in one line. Your challenge. Use a list comprehension to double every number in the list one, two, three, four. Print the new list. You should see two, four, six, eight. Then add an if, to double only the numbers above two. Post your one-liner in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 37.
